articleTitle: What do you think? Spectrum solicits your opinions
Power/energy: Homeostatic control for electric power usage: A new scheme for putting the customer in the control loop would exploit microprocessors to deliver energy more efficiently
abstract: The law of supply and demand works well with much of the world's commerce. Why not apply this law to consumer purchases of electricity? Improbable though this may seem, extensive advances in computation and communication could allow a modified supply-and-demand electrical system to become operational in a few years. Both utilities and customers would benefit. For utilities, there would be opportunities to cut operating costs and capital investments, and for customers there would be options to buy power at lower rates.

articleTitle: Medical electronics II: Seeing speech in real time: The deaf can now view tongue, jaw, and other vocal-tract movements on a CRT display
abstract: Kim is a 3 1/2-year-old profoundly deaf girl who spoke with the high-pitched, effortful sounds so often characteristic of the deaf. With a speech-feedback system called the dynamic orometer, however, she soon mastered speech-reproduction patterns and also began to talk in a relaxed way, in a pitch lowered to the normal childhood range. The orometer is being developed at the University of Alabama in Birmingham.

articleTitle: Computers: Beyond the supercomputer: NASA is developing ultrafast machines to process satellite data that would choke a mere supercomputer
abstract: Computers 1000 times faster than today's fastest supercomputers are needed to process the radar or television pictures satellites will be capable of broadcasting to earth stations in the late 1980s. Computations will be needed on 1013 bits of data every 24 hours — representing at least 500 maps or scenes that satellites will send as they monitor the earth's weather, mineral and water resources, food crops, and atmospheric pollution. The goal, which the National Aeronautics and Space Administration has been attempting to meet since 1971, is to develop a new family of computers: ultrafast image processors that can do up to 1011 operations per second, whereas current computers can do a maximum of 108 such operations. The 1011 operations per second are needed since each picture element (pixel) must be processed at the rate of 102 to 104 operations per second to identify a single map in the required time.

articleTitle: Design case history: speak & spell learns to talk
abstract: Four Texas Instruments engineers, each a specialist in a different field of electronics, got together one day in 1976 at the company's headquarters in Dallas for a brainstorming session. Their aim was simple enough: to develop a new electronic learning aid for children.

Apart from their many other effects, detonated nuclear explosives become coupled to electromagnetic fields and send out electromagnetic pulses (EMPs). To the author's knowledge, the first observation of this effect was on 16 July 1945, by Enrico Fermi at the experimental Trinity explosion. The expanding ionized gases in the fireball displaced the earth's magnetic fields and in this way created electromagnetic radiation. It is now known that EMPs of at least several tens of kilovolts per meter might be generated over wide areas from high-altitude nuclear explosions. Similar and even stronger internally generated EMPs have to be considered in spacecraft. The immediate result is that the electronic memory of an exposed system might be erased. If sufficient energy is concentrated on a semiconductor or on its electrical connections, some of this vital equipment may be permanently wiped out. Today there is almost universal dependence on electronic computers. They are used by first-graders as well as by research engineers. Industry, communications, financial records - all are at stake here. In the event of heavy EMP radiation, I suspect it would be easier to enumerate the apparatus that would continue to function than the apparatus that would stop. In almost all cases, adequate protection can be provided in theory. However, this would entail considerable expense. A final point must be stressed: what is involved in a consideration of EMP is knowledge that, to a great extent, is classified today. The military establishment can take the measures needed for defense because it possesses the classified information. But without widespread dissemination of information to industry - and therefore without actual declassification of essential parts of the EMP discussion - the civilian economy faces the prospects of grinding to a halt in a nuclear encounter.

articleTitle: Communications: Local area nets: A pair of standards: Confronted by marketplace needs, the IEEE 802 Committee is proposing standards for two kinds of networks: Contention access and token passing
abstract: As factories and offices move toward automation, local networks for sharing information and computer-related resources are bound to proliferate. To avoid a veritable Babel as myriad devices built by different manufacturers attempt to communicate, there must be standards for the networks. But which?

articleTitle: Power/energy: Automated power distribution: Increasingly diverse and complex power operation and distribution systems will mean a larger role for microprocessor and communications technologies
abstract: Automating power-distribution systems by microprocessor control and communication technologies, a subject utilities and equipment manufacturers have been investigating and developing for the last 10 years, is a technical answer to the changing economics of production, distribution, and use of electric energy. Rather than managing only the energy supply as they do today ‾ fuel, generation, and transmission ‾ electric utilities will have to control both the supply and the load ‾ the power-distribution system as well as customers' loads.

articleTitle: Consumer electronics: Video games: The electronic big bang
abstract: The video-games industry, the design of game hardware and software, and the psychology of games are examined in this special three-part report.

articleTitle: Medical electronics I: Hearing through sight and feeling: Microelectronic aids to speech and comprehension in the form of visual and tactile devices may soon be available
abstract: Microelectronics is opening new ways for 1.8 million deaf people in the United States to “hear” others. With data processors in a chip, it is now possible to build hearing aids that alter speech according to the individual needs of those with impaired hearing. Training equipment, for example, can make use of a child's sense of sight or touch to teach word pronunciation. Telephone links can be adapted to convert spoken words into printed words on a teletypewriter and vice versa.

articleTitle: Consumer electronics: Video disks: Three choices: Three incompatible approaches to video recording for playback are compared
abstract: A new era in information storage and playback is beginning as video disks and players find their way increasingly into consumers' homes. At about $20, a plastic, mass-produced video disk with a 30-centimeter diameter can carry the equivalent of more than 1010 bits. To store that kind of information for computers, several typical high-density disk-storage systems, or disk packs, would be needed, each using 19 magnetic-disk surfaces and costing about $1000. Furthermore, unlike computer storage systems, consumer video disks do not require elaborate temperature, humidity, and dust controls during operation; they are shipped and handled without special care, like thousands of other products. Of course, the information on a video disk can only be played back. A user cannot record on the disk — at least not yet.

articleTitle: Computers: Computer-aided engineering: Terminals that simulate, test, and debug logic designs promise to change radically the way designers do their jobs
abstract: Computer-aided engineering — a rapidly changing discipline that is much broader than computer-aided design (CAD) — is about to make radical changes in the way electrical engineers do their jobs and companies move products to market. Because these new tools allow engineers to take on more complex projects and to complete those projects faster than before, companies may be able to overcome the problem of ever longer design times in the face of ever shorter product life cycles.

articleTitle: Consumer electronics: Americanizing videotex: Even as U.S. companies prepare to enter the videotex marketplace, what the consumer wants is not yet clear
abstract: Impatient with the droning of the evening newscaster, a man in London hits a button on his TV remote control, and the screen fills with printed bulletins about the latest crisis in Parliament. In a suburb of Paris, a woman uses her TV set to check her bank balance and to call up a list of Club Méditerranée vacations. In a small town in the Netherlands, a boy home sick from school gets his daily lessons sent to him via television. For hundreds of thousands of Europeans, the television set has become a window to reams of information stored in distant computers — news and sports, movie schedules, airline rates, and supermarket specials.

articleTitle: Standards: Antitrust ruling chills standards setting: A U.S. Supreme Court ruling has clouded standards setting with the threat of antitrust liability
abstract: The Supreme Court recently ruled that the American Society of Mechanical Engineers was responsible for the actions of its members who used the ASME standards-interpretation operation to violate antitrust law. The Court approved the assessment of treble damages — more than $7 million — against the ASME, which, it determined, had granted the members involved “apparent authority” to act on its behalf. The members issued an interpretation of a standard, and their interpretation was used by one company to frustrate the sale of a competing device.

articleTitle: Military: Laser weapons: A variety of targets might be neutralized by laser beams, but only if weapons employing them can be utilized with great finesse
abstract: Laser weapons will never be weapons of mass destruction. The largest carbon-dioxide laser ever built produces pulses of only 10-kilojoule energy, the muzzle energy of 20 .45-caliber bullets. However, a prolonged sequence of such pulses, properly focused, could damage satellites at 100 kilometers or more. Laser weapons have been described as “ice pick” weapons: they can neutralize a variety of targets but only if wielded with great finesse.

articleTitle: Education: cracks in the ivory tower: academics are beginning to flee a deteriorating campus environment for jobs in industry - a trend threatening the u.s. technological base
abstract: Call him John Smith. It's not his real name, but that's not important. What is important is his story, which is true.

articleTitle: Software III: Programming for nonprogrammers: New languages are helping those who are not professionally trained to communicate with computers
abstract: The boom in personal computers and the rapid expansion of computing systems built on small computers has brought large numbers of people who are not professional programmers into direct contact with computers. As a result, more and more engineers, businessmen, accountants, and secretaries are discovering how frustrating it can be to get a computer to do what they want it to. Conventional programming languages seem to be too cumbersome, complicated, and time-consuming for easy use by those with little computer training.

articleTitle: Instrumentation:'Seeing' acoustically: New nondestructive techniques permit subsurface examination of materials for density and elasticity
abstract: The acoustic microscope — a new tooi that lets researchers see minute structural details of an object by displaying the object's response to ultrasonic sound — is under development in several laboratories. Athough still in an early stage, the technique has already attained resolutions comparable to those of optical microscopes and is demonstrating its potential in increasing applications, from biomedical research to materials science.

articleTitle: Careers: A skeptic views ethics in engineering: Competing with recession and unemployment for people's concern, ethics still manages to arouse lively debates
abstract: Knowing how fickle human beings are and how short their attention span can be, one would have thought that by now concern with engineering ethics would be on the wane. After all, a decade has passed since Watergate, the Vietnam War, and the onset of the environmental crisis — and also since several prominent civil engineers confessed to bribing the vice president of the United States. And it is 10 years since the scandal at the San Francisco Bay Area Rapid Transit District, in which three engineers were discharged for publicizing inadequacies in the trains' control system, thereby adding “whistle blowing” to the vocabulary of professional engineering.

The U.S. Department of Defense has embarked on the most ambitious — and probably most important — Federal program since the launching of the space exploration program. The VHSIC (Very High Speed Integrated Circuits) program is aimed at developing silicon chips that will be fast enough and reliable enough to ensure continuing U.S. superiority in defense electronics. The six-year program is being financed at $75 million per year and executed by six of the nation's most important corporations.

The image of a robot butler gliding into the dining room and announcing in suitably metallic tones that "dinner is ready" has long been a cliche of science fiction. However, similar computer-synthesized voices, bearing the same message, as well as more informative ones, will soon be heard in thousands of kitchens. A number of United States and Japanese microwave-oven manufacturers have introduced voice-synthesis microprocessors into their top-of-the-line products. Such talking ovens can be programmed to remind home cooks of important steps in preparation at the appropriate times or simply to acknowledge verbally and repeat the settings entered into the oven through its control board.

articleTitle: Communication ICs: The digital evolution in telephony continues: A signal processor furthers distributed switching and monolithic SLICs decrease component count
abstract: While the trend of incorporating more features in communication integrated circuits continued unabated last year, other significant steps were taken to move the integrated services digital network (ISDN) closer to reality. The network, long a visionary plan of the world's major telephone companies, would give each customer in a network a “digital pipe” through which bits would be transmitted to meet all voice, data, and video requirements.

Many vendors now offer specialized small computers called array processors (APs) that are 10 to 1000 times faster than minicomputers or miniframes for many number-crunching applications. But APs. used generally as peripherals to enhance a host minicomputer or mainframe, can pose application and programming problems that many users or designers of conventional computers may find unfamiliar. Because they speed up just a few different operations, these computers are only cost-effective when applied to exactly the right problems and when their programs are best tuned to those problems.

Behind the lens of any recently made consumer camera is electronic automation. To a great extent, smaller and cheaper electronic components have made possible smaller cameras that do more with less human intervention. Today's amateur photographer, even one with little knowledge of f-stops and shutter speeds, can afford a sophisticated camera and take pictures in situations that until recently demanded professional equipment.

articleTitle: Power/energy: Connecting renewable power sources into the system: Windmills, fuel cells, and photovoltaics may serve existing grids, but first many technical, legal, and economic issues must be addressed
abstract: In California, investor windmill farms have sprung up like legendary claim stakes during the gold rush. Like their predecessors, these power prospectors hope to strike it rich. They are selling their wind power to California utilities at profitable rates and are also getting tax benefits on their investments. The utilities benefit, too: they bear none of the equipment investment costs and none of the interconnection costs, and they acquire extra generating capability.

articleTitle: Transportation: France's superfast train: The French National Railroad's fleet of 260-km/h electrics competes favorably with the airlines between Paris and Lyons
abstract: Twenty years of experimentation in design has given France a new train that is superior to the automobile and airplane in speed, safety, comfort, and cost at distances up to 600 kilometers. It is cheaper to ride this train than to drive a car with two passengers over that distance. When the fuel costs for carrying passengers are figured, the train's cost per passenger comes to only one seventh that per passenger on the Airbus, assembled in France by the European consortium Airbus Industrie. The train is the 260-kilometer-per-hour TGV (train à grande vitesse), in service since last September between Paris and Lyons and enormously popular with business travelers.

At about 10 a.m. last May 4, the H.M.S. Sheffield, a British destroyer cruising off the Falkland Islands with 262 sailors aboard, took an Argentine missile amidships and burst into flames. Twenty young men died, and with them died the myth that a big power could emerge unscathed from a head-to-head conflict with a second-rate military power.

articleTitle: Power systems: Hope is rekindled for nuclear energy; new components can reduce power-system operating costs
abstract: Nuclear power expansion in the United States has shown the first signs of recovery from the standstill that followed the Three Mile Island reactor accident in 1979. Last October President Reagan lifted a ban on the reprocessing of spent nuclear fuels that his predecessor, Jimmy Carter, had imposed in 1977 [see “Rebirth for nuclear fuel,” Spectrum, November 1981, pp. 52-57]. The President is also seeking to speed the licensing of new nuclear power plants without compromising their safety, so plants could be planned, designed, built, and operated in 6 to 8 years instead of today's 10 to 14. Three new plants have operated at full power [Table I].

articleTitle: Today's navies: Plying a sea of debate
abstract: When the British learned that the Falkland Islands had been overrun by the Argentine military, they did what countries have been doing for ages. They sent a fleet of warships.

If a war erupted between nations of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the Warsaw Pact, would NATO be prepared to fight it? Leading U.S. military strategists are not sure that question can be answered in the affirmative today, though a flurry of programs are under way to ensure a positive response within several years.

articleTitle: Information control II: Technology transfer at issue: The industry viewpoint: Economics makes industry a cautious ally in academia's fight against U.S. government attempts to stem the free flow of ideas
abstract: The deputy director of the Central Intelligence Agency told scientists and engineers at a meeting of the American Association for the Advancement of Science on Jan. 7, 1982, that they must control the exportation of technical information voluntarily or face legislative action that will “slam shut” the door through which United States expertise is reaching military and economic adversaries.4 “In terms of harm to the national interest,” the CIA official said, “it makes little difference whether the data is copied from technical journals in a library or given away... to an agent of a foreign power.”

articleTitle: Medical electronics III: Rhythmic cues aid lip readers: Through knowledge of the frequency and intensity characteristics of syllables, the deaf can learn to relate speech with text
abstract: A deaf person usually does not recognize the importance of syllable rhythms to understanding speech. But by learning to process rhythmic cues, he or she can often make sense of an otherwise confusing lip reading. A speech-text synchronizer developed at the National Technical Institute for the Deaf, Rochester, N.Y., is intended to train people to understand such cues [Fig. 1].

articleTitle: Innovation: Swan's way: A study in style: With the birth of the electric light bulb, two modern styles of inventing emerged: Thomas Edison's and Joseph Swan's
abstract: Joseph Swan did not invent the light bulb. But then neither did his contemporary, Thomas Edison. The light bulb that Edison demonstrated in Menlo Park, N.J., in 1880 was the climax of an inventive process begun in the early 19th century and involving a multitude of scientists, inventors, and businessmen that included Swan, an outstanding British inventor.

articleTitle: Fiber optics: Single-mode cables and long-wavelength transmission are seen as requisite for next-generation systems
abstract: New fiberoptic technology in the laboratory promises to provide users a long-wavelength option to supplement existing short-wavelength systems. Last year U.S., Canadian, and European telephone companies continued to tie fiber-optic systems operating at the 800-to-900-nanometer-region into existing copper transmission networks. At the same time, engineers were pushing development of fiber-optic components and cables for systems that are expected to transmit at 1300 and 1500 nm. Attempts are being made to perfect methods that would allow fiber-optic components to operate at the longer wavelengths. Separate research in single-mode fibers is also being done. These fibers can transmit light over long distances due to the low loss at the longer wavelengths. Hence single-mode, long-wavelength systems can accommodate a larger bandwidth than multimode, short-wavelength systems.

articleTitle: Industrial electronics: Industry's workhorse gets smarter: The programmable controller adds intelligent input/output modules, block programming in ladder diagram logic, self-diagnosis, and data highways
abstract: Since their introduction in 1969 as electronic replacements for industrial relay panels, programmable controllers (PCs) have widened their functions dramatically. And they have yet to reach their limits. Initially PCs did little more than on-off sequencing of motors, solenoids, and actuators — the principal logic function of the relay panels they replaced. Today they have evolved into intelligent workhorses, with such advanced capabilities as data acquisition and storage, report generation, execution of complex mathematical algorithms, servo motor control, stepping control, axis control, self-diagnosis, system troubleshooting, and “talking” to other PCs and mainframe computers.

articleTitle: Business communications: Local area networks provide an architecture for the expanded use of automated office equipment
abstract: Though transmitted digital data can easily leap over entire continents in milliseconds, it sometimes takes them longer than that to travel the last mile or so within a building. Last year, a number of solutions were offered to this bottleneck in local distribution of data. Communication and computer vendors introduced at least seven local area networks — commonly called LANs — that promise to speed the data flow.

articleTitle: Industrial controls: Computers and microprocessors lead to improvements in batch-process control, motor inverter systems, and industrial laser equipment
abstract: Significant advances in electrotechnology have brought the hope of a fully automated factory a step closer to reality. The developments last year included the design and production of the following: " Batch and sequential process-control systems that can perform several functions within a single system. "Microprocessor-based, load-cornmutated inverter systems that resuit in adjustable-speed ac drives for synchronous motors. The drives are more precise than the mechanical unit they replace. - A design for a fully computer-controlled, solid-state laser system and a new thermally configured ion-laser system that disperses heat faster and more uniformly from the laser plasma.

Ever since World War II, the major military powers have been waging a silent war for control of the “airwaves,” through electronic countermeasures (ECM). Techniques have emerged for disrupting either enemy communications or radar. Infrared and laser systems have been developed to detect or locate targets, guide missiles, or direct artillery fire. With mastery over the airwaves, one side could defeat a more powerful enemy by disrupting the electronic systems that modern military forces depend on.

articleTitle: The U.S. Navy: Can ships survive?
abstract: The war over the Falkland Islands had barely begun when, in a matter of days, both sides lost major warships: the Argentine cruiser General Belgrano and the British destroyer H.M.S. Sheffield. These losses, effected so quickly with so few weapons, have stirred considerable debate about whether surface naval forces can survive the threat of modern weapons, particularly the antiship missile. Are changes in ship design and ship defenses necessary?

articleTitle: Information control I: Technology transfer at issue: The academic viewpoint: Educators believe efforts to limit transfer of knowledge at the university level are likely to weaken the U.S. lead in innovation
abstract: Confronted by increasing commercial competition from Western Europe and Japan in high-technology markets, as well as by heightened tensions in relations with the Soviet Union, the United States has taken a new and vigorous interest in controlling the flow of technology outside its borders. There is growing concern in the Federal government that the “leaking” of technical material and ideas to other nations impairs national security both by diminishing the ability of the U.S. to compete commercially and by reducing the country's edge in armaments. Yet specific efforts that have been initiated to control technology transfer in the university setting are themselves likely to weaken the U.S. position and thus do not serve national interest.

It is inarguable that the Soviets began it all in 1957 when they rocketed a 184-pound satellite named Sputnik into space. It is also clear that the United States caught up and then drew ahead of the USSR in space technology and applications, so that by the 1970s it was the undisputed leader. The U.S. was also seen as an important partner in space ventures by other countries, as well as by the multinational European Space Agency (ESA). But all that is changing. France is now an important entity in the space race, as is Japan. Furthermore, countries who seek partners in space projects no longer turn exclusively to the U.S.

A new development is taking place in military capabilities: with advances in electronics, the emphasis has shifted from delivery vehicles and explosive devices to improvements in sensors, control, and accuracy.

articleTitle: Peace 8: Peace efforts: Broad-based technical and political involvement seems a prerequisite for regional and global security: International approaches to peacekeeping
abstract: The history of mankind has oscillated between periods of conflict and relative peace, with technology contributing to each. Whether with wooden clubs or with missiles in hardened silos, man has used tools to warn perceived enemies to keep clear. And whether spyglass or satellite, tools have been employed to verify that the perceived enemies indeed stay clear. Today perhaps more than ever nations are increasingly dependent on technologies for peace.

articleTitle: Small-business machines: A management-oriented software package and stand-alone information graphics systems are among major new offerings
abstract: Small-business systems offered more of everything last year: more new personal office computers, graphics terminals, desktop minicomputers, and software designed to make programming easier for users. However, the big question of recent years is still on many minds: Will the growing list of office automation products raise the productivity of managers? Managers are reported to represent 80 percent of the costs in the average office, but automation has so far increased productivity largely in the remaining 20 percent of office costs, the clerical and accounting functions. Office systems are spewing out reams of data but relatively little pertinent information for making managerial decisions. The problem, in short, is software. Though signs of progress appeared last year, the surface was barely scratched.

articleTitle: Best bits: Applications of microprocessors: `Flying’ with microprocessors
abstract: The trend toward distributed processing is epitomized by two 16-blt microprocessor systems recently announced by the Link Flight Simulation Division of the Singer Corp. in Binghamton, N.Y. Both systems usa solwer, lass expensive microprocessors to do jobs previously handled by large mainframe computers or minicomputers.

The topic of disarmament currently enjoys a high profile in the popular press, presumably because there is a great populist concern about the prospects of nuclear war that did not exist a few years ago. This broader concern by the public is counterbalanced by a slowing of progress in disarmament negotiations at the governmental level and by an escalation in size of nuclear arsenals, particularly those of the U.S. and the Soviet Union.

The consensus of the experts is that remote sensing by satellite is by far the most effective technology that can be used in the interests of peacekeeping. As the power of satellite systems to identify ground-based military equipment and facilities increases, the need for on-site inspections to verify treaty conformance may decrease to the point where it is no longer an issue.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Computer and math anxiety
abstract: The debate about the relative mathematical ability of males and females goes on. The experts are not of one mind as to whether there exists a biologically induced difference. The evidence of such a difference seems scarce or nonexistent. On the other hand, there is little disagreement that there are environmental factors that cause women as a group to perform less well in mathematics than do males. Simply put, if one does not study math, one does not do well in math. And there are many attitudinal and motivational factors that cause women to avoid mathematical studies. The unfortunate result is that math serves as a critical filter in screening out countless women from engineering careers. A 1980 report showed 66 percent of high school males who were college-bound had completed four years of math, in contrast to only 44 percent of the college-bound females. Male SAT scores in mathematics averaged 48 points higher than female scores.

articleTitle: Military/aerospace systems: NASA shuttle successes mark a year of transition; meanwhile, military programs are revitalized
abstract: It was the climax of the most sophisticated research-and-development effort ever undertaken in aerospace technology: the launching and landing of the U.S. Space Shuttle Columbia. Twice in 1981 the missions proved not only that the shuttle was flightworthy, but also that it was reusable. It was the beginning, some said, of a new era of near-earth space applications. At the same time another era — that of U.S. exploration of the planets — saw one of the last in a long line of spectacular successes.

articleTitle: Instrumentation: Computer-aided troubleshooting becomes easier and faster; automated testing of VLSI circuits poses challenges
abstract: Instruments teamed with microcomputers and minicomputers last year to ease the problems of designers and production engineers in testing increasingly complicated electronic equipment. The computers can either be built into the measuring instruments themselves or the instruments can be interfaced with the computers or with calculators through bus-connected systems.

articleTitle: War 2: Today's arsenals: The modern army, navy, and air force turn to the technologies that can ensure a battlefield edge: Today's armies: Plodding toward automation
abstract: Tanks have increased army mobility, cannons and missiles have increased firepower, and radio and telephone have increased cohesion, but, in the U.S. Army, the foot soldier still makes up between one quarter and one half of the total fighting strength. And much the same is true for every other major nation's army today. Some experts contend that nuclear weapons, chemical and biological warfare, and guerilla tactics have made the traditional infantry obsolete. But wars continue to be won or lost by foot soldiers — the conflicts in the South Atlantic and between Iran and Iraq are two examples. So technologically sophisticated nations are trying to develop and field machines that will wean the common soldier from his rifle and take him off his feet.

articleTitle: War 3: Technology in the military: Command, control, and communications along with countermeasures and intelligence offer some solutions: Strategic C3: A goal unreached
abstract: Command, control, and communications (C<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>) are the brains and nervous system of any modern military force. articleTitle: Video: On the shopping list of equipment are a new video-disk system and an electronic video still camera
abstract: A plethora of video home-entertainment products went to market last year to compete for the shrinking consumer dollar. Among the more significant developments were the following: • Sony demonstrated a prototype of a filmless video 3S-millimeter camera that takes still pictures for viewing on a conventional televisionscreen. • A new video-disktechnologymaterializedin a system from the VietorCo. of Japan. in sophistication it fallsbetweenlaser-based systems, from such companies as Magnavox, and RCA's capacitance electronicdisk, which uses a stylus. • More video-tape recorders were introduced in the equally popular Beta and VHS formats. In somecasesthe recorder cannowbeenclosedin the cameracase, thusmakingthe unit evenmore portable. • A number of companies introduced advanced projection televisionsystems, with fine-tuning of color convergence circuits producing a clearer picture. One entry from the Zenith Radio Corp. solvesthe convergence problem through innovativedesign of the color tubes [see Spectrum, November 1981, pp 40-45].

articleTitle: C3 gets a vote of confidence
abstract: Just about a year and a half ago, with the change of administration, my term as assistant secretary of defense for command, control, communications, and intelligence (C<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>I) ended. In view of the continued concern expressed in the media, an update of arguments to support that confidence is in order.

The attraction video games have for some players borders on addiction: What are the psychological factors that incite people to play video games, and what may be the implications of widespread game play?

For this reason the U.S. Department of Defense and the State Department want to prevent hardware, software, and information that could aid the Russians from falling into their hands.
