Military intelligence — timely information about an actual or potential enemy — is pulled together from widely disparate sources. At one time it was gathered by ears and eyes, communicated by word of mouth, and interpreted in the minds of experts. Although this is still practised today, electronic intelligence gathering and computer analysis are stealing the limelight. These days the ears and eyes are in the sky, in space, and under the ocean; electromagnetic waves are the primary information source, and computers transform the data for the experts into meaningful intelligence.

articleTitle: Best bits: Applications of microprocessors: Making the shuttle reliable
abstract: The U.S. space Shuttle's robot arm, used to manipulate equipment carried in the shuttle's cargo bay, is controlled by one of six computers on board. However engineers at Spar Aerospace Ltd. of Ontario, Canada, designed the arm with a microprocessor that monitors the computer and the robot arm's electronics. The device, manufactured by the Rockwell International Corp. of Downey, Calif, contlnually checks for malfunctions and faulty commands.

articleTitle: War 5: U.S. readiness: Preparedness of the U.S. military is discussed in essays by an incumbent and three former military leaders; a fifth essay analyzes industry's role: The U.S army: Is it ready?
abstract: Although advanced technologies clearly have the potential to improve U.S. military posture, have they been contributing all they could? In the following pages, military experts look at the current state of the U.S. fighting machine, examining in various contexts its readiness for combat.

articleTitle: The U.S. Air Force: Is it vulnerable?
abstract: Suppose war broke out in Europe today. Could the U.S. Air Force successfully enter enemy territory, knock out heavily defended airfields, and win in air-to-air combat with Soviet pilots? Probably not, says Lieutenant General John T. Chain Jr., the Air Force's deputy chief of staff for plans and operations. In a speech last spring before 300 of the nation's top military officials and industrialists at an Air Force Association symposium, Gen. Chain warned of deficiencies that put U.S. pilots at a disadvantage.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: You said it, we didn't
abstract: In the January issue we asked readers what they think of Spectrum, and they told us.

The United States is spending billions of dollars a year for military equipment but many believe it is not getting its money's worth. For years, it has produced fewer and fewer military planes, ships, guns, radar, and other equipment while paying more and more real dollars for them. In addition to the problem of force modernization, the combat readiness of the armed forces has been declining.

articleTitle: Consumer electronics: Stereophonic sound for television: Three transmission systems, vying for selection as the U.S. standard, are compared
abstract: In many parts of Japan and West Germany, a television viewer hears stereo sound while watching a program. In the United States, by contrast, a viewer hears monophonic sound. But soon, possibly by late 1983, TV broadcasters in the United States will begin transmitting stereo sound for the audio portion of selected TV programs. This sound will have quality comparable to that now transmitted by FM radio stations. But first, stereo-TV transmission standards must be set.

articleTitle: Best bits: Applications of microprocessors: Smart heart
abstract: A microprocessor-regulated mechanical heart is Co be implanted In a calf this summer at the University of Utah to demonstrate that the rigid titanium two-chamber pump can sustain life.

articleTitle: Peace 7: Threats to peace: Scenarios of war that worry experts include accidental nuclear exchanges and escalating brushfire wars
abstract: In a television dramatization reaching the homes of millions of Americans a few months ago, Edward Teller, often referred to as the father of the hydrogen bomb, was pictured standing in a Los Alamos, N.M., living room before J. Robert Oppenheimer, sometimes called the father of the atomic bomb. Dr. Teller was holding in his hand a petition signed by many engineers and scientists and sent to him by the physicist Leo Szilard. It called on the U.S. government to demonstrate an atomic bomb publicly The hope was that the Japanese would surrender if they witnessed the destructive power of the bomb, thereby saving thousands of lives. Though inclined to sign it, Dr. Teller wanted his director's permission.

articleTitle: Design case history: the `infinite' matrix printer
abstract: Before 1975, matrix printers were a cheap fix - low in price and poor in quality. They were bought by those who wanted to print large quantities of text from a host computer without spending the money for an expensive daisywheel printer. Manufacturers of matrix printers were also content to aim their product at the low end of the market, because the design of matrix printers seemed inherently limiting. Royden C. Sanders Jr. changed all that.

The reader will find in this annual review a wealth of information covering the state of the art in hardware end software and ranging from devices to systems. Over the past several months, a few outstanding trends have been reinforced. The “digitization of America” (and other advanced nations) is continuing with little indication of a slowdown. Very large-scale integration promises to enhance this digital trend as it enables the wedding of computers and instrumentation and the wider dispersal of computer power to nooks and crannies previously unthought of. The computer is thus insinuating its way into everything from electronic funds transfer and the power utilities to the factory floor.

In this column last month we touched upon the problem of underutilization of engineering personnel, suggesting, among other things, that it is at least partly the responsibility of the engineer to help design his or her own job. Specifically, we said that many engineers feel they are being used as technicians, and we suggested there's no better place to begin shifting the interface than at the interface itself. Shouldn't the engineer, and the engineering supervisor, take the initiative to upgrade the functions of both technician and engineer, we asked.

In the June Spectral Lines we discussed some of the factors involved in arms control. In particular, we spoke of the concept of a global information cooperative that would use a series of earth-orbiting, intelligence-gathering satellites. We also mentioned studies by the International Federation of Automatic Control that would consider the international political arena as a system that might be modeled so as to teach methods of promoting stability. We mentioned the difficulties of such projects and the skepticism with which they are met. Yet as an alternative to continuing arms escalation they seem worthy of further consideration.

Pilots landing at major airports use the instrument landing system (ILS) to guide them onto the runway in bad weather. Many small airports, however, do not have ILS. Pilots must determine from observation whether their approach is high or low, and in bad weather visibility may be limited.

The history of warfare has been marked by an overwhelming expectation that when a weapon was launched it would not hit its target. In the case of rifle fire during the Civil War in the United States, the odds in favor of a miss were about 100 000 to 1. In air-to-ground bombing in World War II (except in instances of area bombing), the odds in favor of a miss were still on the order of 20 to 1. Even in the early days of missile development, the unstated goal of those working on the V-2 rocket was simply to make it a more dangerous situation to be at the target than to be at the launch point.

Arms-control agreements are not a complete approach to peace, and they cannot by themselves resolve conflicting interests among nations. They can, however, reduce immediately available means for violence and thus foster more diligent searches for nonviolent ways to reconcile interests.

Mainframes inched ahead in performance in 1981-a familiar trend ever since the beginning of computer time - while superminicomputers got more "super" and therefore became the equal of some mainframes. Distinctions have blurred all along the line; several microcomputer systems today are equivalent to low-end minicomputers, and a microcomputer system from one manufacturer - billed as a "micromainframe" - is equivalent in some configurations to a low-end mainframe [see Microprocessors, p. 32].

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Dead end - whose fault?
abstract: Listen to this, from the op ed page of a recent issue of The New York Times: "It is exquisite boredom. We arrive for work at 8 in the morning and stuff envelopes until 4:30 in the afternoon. To help get us through another day of mindless labor, my fellow workers and I listen to the radio, discuss our personal lives and interests, complain about the lousy wages, and, by midafternoon, struggle to stay awake. On the slowest days, we vie for a chance to get out and run an errand, like hungry dogs fighting over a scrap of meat.

Alfred Nobel — the Swedish inventor of dynamite — having considered the inherent danger of his invention as applied to warfare established in 1901 the Nobel prizes, recognizing individuals who contributed to peace either directly or through advances in science and medicine. He saw in science and technology those elements that would enhance the welfare and well-being of mankind, thereby reducing some of the causes of war.

articleTitle: Discrete devices: Fabrication and processing techniques, borrowed from LSI technology, play major roles in new component designs
abstract: Materials processing and fabrication techniques, some of them similar to those used in large-scale integration, have made possible the production of denser, smaller, and faster components during the past year. Among the components were high-frequency power-switching devices [see “Switching lots of watts at high speeds,” by B.J. Baliga, Spectrum, December 1981, pp. 43-481, microwave devices for communications, solid-state relays for applications formerly performed by electromechanical relays, and isolation amplifier transformers.

The fate of the Clinch River breeder reactor project in Oak Ridge, Tenn., continues to be a seesaw struggle between Congress and the White House. In 1977, when President Jimmy Carter moved to kill the proposed $3.2 billion fast-breeder project by halting environmental hearings, Congress voted funds to keep it alive. Now, with President Reagan supporting the reactor, construction is threatened by opposition in Congress.

Public apprehension about the possibility of nuclear war continues to mount. In a poll of 1420 adults across the U.S. taken by the New York Times and CBS News Poll May 19-23, 43 percent said it was “fairly likely” or “very likely” that the U.S. would become involved in a nuclear war within the decade. Soon after, U.S. Department of Defense policy makers made the public aware of a five-year defense plan that assumes nuclear conflict with the USSR could be protracted and defines the strategy for fighting such a nuclear war. Part of that strategy, for example, would be reliance on the so-called decapitation principle - that is, strikes aimed at political and military leadership and communications lines.

articleTitle: War 1: The force multiplier: Advanced technology, and particularly electronics, provides leverage in modern military defense systems
abstract: Just weeks after the British ran into unexpected technological difficulties in their battle against Argentina for the Falklands [see previous pages], Israel destroyed an estimated 90 Syrian planes and 19 Syrian SAM-7 antiaircraft missile sites with hardly a loss themselves. How was this lopsided victory over advanced Soviet-built equipment accomplished?

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Walking the technology-transfer tightrope
abstract: Historians tell us that, in the United States at least, the need to protect information about military technology was virtually nonexistent prior to 1860. Before that, all adversaries used essentially identical weapons, so there were no secrets. But during the Civil War torpedoes and mines arrived on the scene. Inventors had a field day devising ingenious designs, and although many of them were never reduced to practice, military and naval leaders were concerned about keeping both real and potential designs from the enemy.

articleTitle: Personal computers/calculators: New units do more and cost less; peripheral interfaces further extend their capabilities
abstract: Faced with a sluggish consumer market, the large manufacturers of personal computers shifted gears last year and concentrated less on attracting home users and more on small-business proprietors interested in financial applications. More financial software was added for Apple computers and for Radio Shack's TRS-80 series, the workhorses in this field.

Summary form only given. The hardware shown here is discussed in articles he lie pter throughout the issue. Spectrum chose these major systems of the US Army, Navy, and Air Force to give an idea of relative sizes and costs.

It is reported that the Israeli minister of defense was able to watch the most recent battle in Lebanon unfurl on his own television monitor (see Aviation Week & Space Technology, June 5, 1982, p. 16). He attributed his country's success against air attack to its military communications system. This case is testimony to the need felt by both major powers and smaller nations like Israel for increasingly sophisticated command, control, and communications (C<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>) systems used to command complex weaponry, from smart missiles to laser-guided artillery [see p. 96].

A promising new microcomputer system, developed by researchers at Texas A&M University, College Station, can automatically detect and de-energize downed nigh-power cables that might otherwise thrash about for hours on the ground, creating severe safety hazards. The system is proposed for installation in utility substations, where high-voltage “mains” branch out into low-voltage “feeders.”

articleTitle: Audio: High-fidelity sound emanates from smaller, modular systems; innovations are seen in tape recorders and turntables
abstract: Until recently many audiophiles assumed that high fidelity could be achieved only with large, bulky equipment. Squeezing audio technology into anything smaller than a breadbox degraded performance, they felt. Since the introduction of Sony's Walkman stereo audio-cassette player two years ago, other manufacturers have also packed higher-performing hi-fi into smaller enclosures. What's more, all of the smaller units needed to put together a hi-fi system are now available from the same manufacturer Formerly, customers had to hunt among different manufacturers for the best combination of tuner, amplifier, turntable, tape deck, and speakers.

articleTitle: Industrial electronics: Our computers aren't speaking: Innovation in computer-based manufacturing has led to a pressing need for interface standards
abstract: Picture a manufacturing plant composed of skilled workers and management personnel, none of whom speak the same language. The company's products may get manufactured, but probably not very efficiently. This roughly is the problem that industries face as they rely more and more on incompatible computer-based devices to raise productivity. This situation is pushing the development of standards that will open up the communication roadblocks.

Both the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the Warsaw Pact have deployed thousands of nuclear weapons in European nations for use if war breaks out. Current NATO doctrine includes the use of nuclear weapons in the early stages of such a battle if NATO appears to be losing. Would the vast quantities of electronics deployed by the United States and its allies survive on such a battlefield?

articleTitle: International arms transfers: Imports and exports
abstract: Throughout the 1970s, the United States supplied 45 percent of the major weapons imported by Third World countries and the Soviet Union supplied about 27 percent. During the same decade, however, Western European arms producers began competing seriously for the Third World market, and the arms industries of several Third World countries grew as well.<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">∗</sup>

articleTitle: Microprocessors: Design case history: Biomation's logic analyzer: An old lesson is relearned: Utility for users, rather than product sophistication, is key to success
abstract: The plane ride home from Wescon '76, Los Angeles, should have been joyous for the marketing team from Biomation Inc. It wasn't. The company had just announced two microprocessor-based logic analyzers, the 1650-D and the 168-D. The 1650-D, which was about what everyone had expected, appeared to be a winner. But the 168-D, a bold incursion by the Santa Clara, Calif., company into a market segment previously the domain of giant Hewlett-Packard Co., was in trouble. Compared with what HP had introduced at Wescon '76, the Biomation 168-D palled.

articleTitle: The rapid-deployment force: How it should work
abstract: During the Vietnam War the United States committed so many resources to Southeast Asia that it pillaged its capability to defend Western Europe. Now it has forced the pendulum back the other way, spending huge sums during the last decade in preparation for a conflict in Europe that will probably never occur. What is apt to take place — perhaps even within the next six months or year — is a conventional war in Southwest Asia, or Latin America, or Africa.

articleTitle: War 6: Future weaponry: Trends in military R&D are reviewed by present and former U.S. defense officials; an expert comments on communications in space: Research thrusts of the U.S. DoD
abstract: The fragility of humans and the shortcomings of their senses are likely to be less significant in future conflicts than they have been in the past. Remote probes and satellites have replaced human scouts; radars and sonars have replaced eyes and ears; digital transmissions are replacing the voice; and computers are replacing the human brain — in speed if not in reasoning ability. Electronics is changing the face of war — further dehumanizing it, perhaps; automating it, certainly.

articleTitle: Space systems: Can they withstand attack?
abstract: Military space systems are not weapons themselves, but they do provide streams of data — in meteorology, warning and surveillance, navigation, and communication — that commanders need to make more effective use of their weapons. The growing military reliance on space systems makes it necessary to ensure that these systems can continue to function through all levels of conflict, even a protracted nuclear war.

Readers tell us how we're doing in many ways. Some write letters, a few of which find their way into the Forum column. Others telephone us, particularly if an article or other editorial item hits home in an especially positive or negative way. But by far the most responses — numbering in the thousands for each issue — come in the form of “votes” cast using the reader service cards on the back of each issue. These votes are tallied and are used by the editors as guides in their coverage of specific topics in future issues. Though a low response rate for a certain article does not mean we won't publish articles on that same topic again, it does mean that we'll try to determine the reason for the low vote, perhaps approaching the topic differently the next time around, or possibly we won't run articles on that topic as frequently as we had planned.

With a compact microprocessorcontrolled unit, the household cook who also holds an outside job wlli soonbe able to start the evening roast while driving home. Such remote cooking will be possible when the Kitchen Controller from West Bend Co., West Bend, Wis., reachesretail stores.

articleTitle: Microprocessors: Progress is reported in programming, speed, complexity, and versatility; new 32-bit devices are announced
abstract: As the microprocessor marked its 10th anniversary in 1981, four different 32-bit designs were unveiled — an indicator that development and growth have not slowed in this seasoned technology. The new designs were: (1) Intel Corp.'s long-awaited iAPX 432 micromainframe, a three-chip set in HMOS, with the design emphasis on high-level-language (Ada) programmability; (2) Hewlett-Packard Co.'s single-chip NMOS microprocessor with 450 000 transistors, designed for a maximum speed of 18 megahertz and dissipating nearly 7 watts; (3) Bell Laboratories' Bellmac-32, a single-chip microprocessor fabricated in twin-tub CMOS technology that dissipates less than 1 W and uses new “domino” circuits that operate at twice the speed of previous CMOS circuits; and (4) Nippon Telegraph and Telephone's CMOS microprocessor fabricated with 2-micrometer line widths enabling 20 000 gates to be packed on a chip only 12 millimeters square and dissipating only 750 milliwatts.

Starting a nuclear war with the object of winning seems an idea whose time — if it ever came — has passed. No longer can the United States or the Soviet Union hope to attain any military or political advantage by threatening a nuclear first strike against the other or even by carrying out such a threat. Inevitable and unacceptable retaliation rules out a sane decision by either superpower to strike first. The sole remaining value of a nuclear force is to deter the other side from using its own nuclear capability.

A vast array of sensors have been placed in earth orbit in the last 10 years. Passive sensors in the optical, infrared, and microwave portions of the spectrum have been returning data on geological resources, land-use patterns, soil moistures, and sea and ice conditions. Since 1978, active microwave sensors - scatterometers and altimeters - have been measuring sea surface winds and sea roughness. But the newest "eyes" in space - synthetic-aperture radars, or SARs - utilized some of the most sophisticated sensor technology ever flown in orbit.

articleTitle: Software I: Function-level computing: A new programming method, linked to radically different architectures, may greatly simplify software development
abstract: Computer hardware has advanced tremendously in the last 25 years, going from vacuum tubes to very large-scale integrated circuits. In the same period neither the architecture of computers nor the programming languages used to control them have changed significantly. As a result, the expanding capabilities of VLSI are not being fully exploited and the costs of much-needed programs are soaring. Recognition of this fact has focused attention on a style of programming called functional programming, which offers the prospect of much cheaper programs and new machine architectures that exploit VLSI. The functional approach rejects the model of computing conceived by the mathematician John von Neumann and others. The von Neumann model is based on a computer consisting of a central processing unit (CPU), a store or memory, and a connection between them that transmits a single unit of data, or “word,” between the CPU and the store. Because today's programming languages are modeled on such computers, programs are complex, concerned with the smallest data entities, and seldom reusable in building new programs.

articleTitle: Computer-aided design: Automating chip layout: New computer-based layout systems are faster than their human counterparts and produce designs that almost match those created manually
abstract: Only a small portion of new large-scale and very large-scale integrated-circuit designs are laid out automatically today. But that picture is changing. IC fabrication costs are now so low that the design process offers the only major avenue for reducing IC costs further. IC producers are certain to adopt automated layout tools — sophisticated programs that translate functional specifications into physical descriptions of chips — increasingly over the next few years, and by 1990 layout will probably be predominantly automatic.

articleTitle: Computers: Computing at the speed limit: Computers 1000 times faster than today's supercomputers would benefit vital scientific applications
abstract: Unheralded efforts in the United States, mainly in universities, have removed major stumbling blocks to building cost-effective superfast computers for scientific and engineering applications within five years. These computers would have sustained speeds of billions of floating-point operations per second (flops), whereas with the fastest machines today the top sustained speed is only 25 million flops, with bursts to 160 megaflops.

About eight months ago several students at the University of California at Berkeley confounded their elders in the computer science department: they found a simple programming trick with which to bypass security checks in the university timesharing systems so they could either intercept electronic mail meant for staff members or steal system files. Although the students told university officials of their discovery - and so no harm may have been done - their easy penetration of a supposedly secure computer system was just one of at least a thousand computer breakins that have been reported in the past several years, most of them in timesharing systems, according to several computer security specialists.

articleTitle: Solid state: Integrated optoelectronics: The marriage of lasers, detectors, and transistors in a single monolithic package promises fact, reliable data transmission
abstract: Advances in the fabrication of electronic and optical devices ‾ transistors as well as lasers and photodetectors ‾ make it possible to combine the two types of devices into one circuit to create a new, powerful class of monoiithically integrated circuits for optical communications.

articleTitle: Space and aeronautics: An alternative launching medium: Accelerating payloads by electromagnetic force may one day prove an alternative to conventional rockets
abstract: Space exploration from Sputnik to the space shuttle has thus far relied mostly on one technology for getting payloads into space: chemical rockets. However, a possible alternative is beginning to emerge that would not only be cheaper, but could also find application in antitank and antiaircraft weapons and thermonuclear fusion. That alternative is the use of electromagnetic force to launch large payloads at high velocity. Though full-scale development of these electromagnetic launchers is still far off and significant problems remain unsolved, early results from laboratory models are impressive.

articleTitle: Computer software: Software design: Breaking the bottleneck: A visionary approach is recommended in place of the piecemeal policy now in effect
abstract: The software design crisis, the extraordinary manpower cost of programming new information systems, could be eased by 1990 — or it could last until the year 2020. It all depends on whether computer developers adopt a visionary approach that actively seeks a fully integrated programming support system, or whether they continue the present ultracautious, piecemeal development.

articleTitle: Solid state: VHSIC: A status report: The first two years of the program's lifespan is viewed by some as gestation and others as incubation. When will the baby walk?
abstract: With more than $400 million pledged for research and development over six years, the Very High-Speed Integrated Circuits (VHSIC) program of the U.S. Department of Defense is certainly the most ambitious and probably the most important Federal program since the United States embarked upon space exploration a quarter of a century ago. Up to now, the DOD has relied mainly on methods developed during World War II to organize and operate its aircraft, tanks, ships, and weapons-delivery systems. The radically altered future toward which VHSIC is rapidly leading is one in which there will be a pervasive dependence on electronics, and thus on very large-scale integration (VLSI), in all defense operations. Modifications will be needed in operating systems, work-force commitments, training, logistics, and, above all, management of the military establishment.

articleTitle: Power/energy: Thyristors: Future workhorses in power transmission: Research is under way to cut energy losses and costs and to improve reliability
abstract: During the last few years the use of power electronics in electric-utility transmission and distribution systems is increasing significantly along with thyristor capabilities. High-power thyristors that can pass up to 3000 amperes and withstand, when turned off, up to 5000 volts are under development.

articleTitle: Computers: Products that talk: Speech-synthesis devices are being incorporated into dozens of products as difficult technical problems are solved
abstract: Speech synthesis, the production of intelligible speech from computer data, is no longer a novelty. Text-to-speech products with unlimited vocabulary are available as automated readers for the blind, and in the next two years they will be incorporated into telephone-based inquiry systems that will give users access to data bases from any phone. Though these devices do not yet have fully natural-sounding speech, their quality is improving rapidly. Speech chips with limited vocabulary are already at a quality level comparable to that of tape recorders. They can create phrases from 200 or 300 preselected words and are rapidly moving into all applications where taped messages might be used. Such progress is based on the transformation of relatively slow and elaborate laboratory algorithms into fast and cheap commercial ones.

articleTitle: Air traffic control: Automating U.S. air lanes: A review: The Federal Aviation Administration's new 20-year plan to modernize air traffic control faces rough weather
abstract: The Federal Aviation Administration has proposed an ambitious $9 billion plan to modernize and eventually automate the U.S. air traffic control system over the next 20 years. The plan, announced last January, calls for replacing IBM 9020 computers in en-route traffic centers with new and more powerful systems, automating ground-air communications systems, and replacing very high- and ultrahigh-frequency instrument landing systems with microwave landing systems. After 1990, all critical air traffic control (ATC) functions are to be fully automated, considerably reducing the number of necessary air traffic controllers.

articleTitle: Power/energy: Wind turbines at work: High-capacity wind machines are being integrated with the electric power grid in oil-dependent, wind-rich areas
abstract: Multimegawatt wind-turbine generators are becoming a commercial reality. Electric power systems in California and Hawaii, for example, are already committed to the exploitation of wind energy. Several manufacturers are developing advanced wind-turbine generators, and a few have delivered such machines to users.

articleTitle: Technology: Holography: A reassessment: Holography enjoys a modest but secure and steadily growing position in areas, among others, such as nondestructive testing
abstract: After the initial hoopla and the inevitable reaction to exaggerated expectations, holography has emerged as neither the scientific panacea its rabid supporters envisioned nor the technological dud its detractors predicted. Rather, it has become established as a basic technology in a variety of fields. In some applications holographic techniques are now indispensable. And prospects for expansion are bright, although some of the more glamorous uses, such as three-dimensional television, may be farther away than originally thought.

articleTitle: VLSI/LSI components: ICs are denser and faster than was thought achievable through state-of-the-art processing and computer-aided design
abstract: The seemingly endless flow of new solid-state devices continued — dynamic and static RAMs, innovative program memories, faster circuits, gate arrays, and more — while surprisingly high integrated-circuit densities were achieved with state-of-the-art processing and computer-aided design, both of which had been criticized widely as inadequate for the job.

articleTitle: Power/energy: Renewable energy: Target for 2050: Massive capital investment, international cooperation, and technical breakthroughs will be key in attaining this goal
abstract: The opportunities for supplying all the world's future energy needs already exist. What is lacking is imagination, entrepreneur-ship, and leadership to take advantage of them. World leaders are needed who can articulate the goal and sell it, engineers and scientists who can do the technical planning and implementation, managers who can operate on the scale needed, and entrepreneurs who are willing to put capital on the line. Most important, farsighted politicians must be found who are willing to cooperate across national borders.

articleTitle: Military: Radar: Shield or target? Costly radar being developed by the U.S. may give an opponent a decisive advantage by broadcasting the position and makeup of forces
abstract: It is fashionable in some military circles to belittle infantrymen as deficient for not availing themselves of all the latest technology. But this much is sure: no sane infantryman engaged in heavy combat would run to the top of a nearby hill, light a flare, and dare the enemy to hit him. Yet some $50 billion a year of the United States defense budget goes to develop, buy, and support radar systems that do the electronic equivalent of exactly that. For 20 years, many in the U.S. defense establishment have been aware of this problem but have swept it under the rug.

articleTitle: Nuclear power: Control-room design: Lessons from TMI: Improved instrumentation plus computer-based decision aids under development should help minimize the potential consequences of accidents
abstract: Control-room operators in the Crystal River nuclear power plant in Gainesville, Fla., were going about their routine tasks on Feb. 26, 1980, when warning lights began to flash. It was 2:23 p.m. A malfunction had led to the loss of most of the important control-room instruments needed for operator action. Wiihin a minute, the nuclear reactor shut itself off, as it had been designed to do in an emergency. As during the 1979 Three Mile Island-2 accident, the power-operated relief valve was stuck open, and coolant water was escaping into the containment building. Unlike TMI, however, the potentially dangerous situation did not develop into a significant accident. Even though much of the instrumentation malfunctioned, the operators were able to shut a blocked valve and stop the loss of reactor coolant through the relief valve. By 3:15 p.m. they had brought the reactor to a shutdown.

articleTitle: Power/energy: The supereiectrification of Brazil: A huge hydroelectric complex under construction at Itaipu plus planned long-distance transmission lines signal the country's ambitions
abstract: How can a rapidly industrializing and urbanizing country that is nearly as big as the United States but lacks cheap, high-quality fossil fuels meet the ever-growing electricity needs of 120 million inhabitants? For Brazil, which fills this description, there was one obvious answer: by turning to its vast hydroelectric resources.

articleTitle: Software II: Automating programming: Researchers are beginning to shift the growing burden of programming to the computer itself
abstract: Though some researchers consider radical changes in the way computers work to be essential to break the programming bottleneck, such an approach inevitably will take a number of years to bear fruit. In the meantime, others are working on more evolutionary approaches: leaving the computers as they are but automating the tedious job of programming them. In essence, these computer scientists are taking the development of programming languages one step further. Twenty years ago Fortran and other high-level languages were developed to enable programmers to generate many machine-language commands from fewer high-level instructions. Today's efforts are aimed at producing languages that will allow a simple statement about the purpose or behavior of a program to generate the entire high-level language algorithm to carry out the operations, thus eliminating the need for applications progammers.

articleTitle: We look at ourselves: How to make it big: Engineers as entrepreneurs: Abandoning a secure job and regular paycheck may seem like jumping from a plane without a parachute. What makes engineers leap?
abstract: You are a successful engineer who works for a company. Have you ever left a meeting with your manager, feeling frustrated with corporate bureaucracy and dreaming of starting your own company so you could manage it in a way that made sense? Have you ever perceived a surefire marketing opportunity — a niche so obvious that it seemed amazing no one had jumped in to exploit it? Did you ever fail to convince management to develop a unique system you were certain was a winner, tempting you to quit and make the product yourself?

articleTitle: Communications: Greater message capacity for satellites: Techniques such as the use of new frequencies, digital encoding, and bandwidth compression will increase mission efficiency
abstract: The satellite communication techniques that have allowed dramatic growth in services in the last 15 years are nearing their useful limits. These techniques have relied on increases in both power and bandwidth as each new satellite has been placed in orbit. Some satellites in a geostationary arc are now only about 3° apart, and some arcs are already crowded. Newly allocated frequency bands need more advanced technological developments to be useful. Because power is related to mass, powerful satellites for geostationary orbit are limited by expendable launch-vehicle capacity of about 1300 kilograms per satellite.

articleTitle: Automotive electronics: Drivers get more options in 1983: Car makers embrace electronics in an all-out drive to improve performance, handling, fuel economy, riding quality, driver aids, and entertainment
abstract: Ten microprocessors, 94 integrated circuits, 123 active components, and 891 passive components: this is the electronic content of a typical 1983 Cadillac Seville equipped with a 4.1-liter V-8 engine and numerous options. The era of electronics in cars has arrived. Car makers now ask, “What electronic applications will customers accept and pay for?” No longer do they question whether electronic technology can do the job.

articleTitle: Finding the flaws in nuclear power plants
abstract: Premature pinholes in the steam generator tubing of the Indian Point 3 nuclear power plant in New York State and vibration-induced wear of the Ringhals 3 nuclear steam generator in Sweden have one thing in common: they are typical of a worldwide rash of similar aging problems that are shutting down reactors or forcing them to operate at reduced power. And wherever nuclear plants remain down for inspection and repair, consumers storm at the resulting utility rate increases to cover the purchase of replacement power. To meet the problem, fresh nondestructive evaluation (NDE) techniques are being devised to give earlier warning of troubles that may threaten public safety or plant availability.

articleTitle: Information control: The dilemma of technology transfer: Industry-Government cooperation is sought in developing priorities for the protection of technical information developed in the U.S.
abstract: When six Japanese engineers were arrested in California last June 22 for allegedly buying IBM trade secrets from an undercover FBI agent and warrants were obtained for the arrest of 12 other persons in Japan, the problem of illegal export of U.S. technical information became public in a forceful way. If U.S. high-technology companies are tempting targets for the Japanese, then they must be irresistible for Soviet agents working to close the technological gap between East and West.

articleTitle: Solid state: Rethinking the 256-kb RAM: Creativity in the factory may be more important than innovation in product design
abstract: Now that the Japanese dominate the market for 64-K dynamic random-access memories, will they also crowd out United States competitors in the market for 256-kilobit RAMs? At least two Japanese companies ‾ Hitachi Ltd. and Fujitsu Ltd., both in Tokyo ‾ will start commercial production of 256-kbchips as soon as 1983, two years earlier than most industry observers had predicted and at least one year earlier than U.S. merchant companies. Hitachi is already the leading supplier of 64-K chips, with 40 percent of the international market, while Fujitsu ranks second with 20 percent of the market, according to Dataquest Inc., market researchers in Cupertino, Calif.

articleTitle: Communications: Low-power television: Short-range, low-cost TV stations are in the offing as the FCC prepares to establish broadcast requirements
abstract: Stations that operate at power levels of only 10 to 1000 watts instead of many hundreds of kilowatts promise to do for television in the United States what FM did for radio: provide local outlets for special interests, minorities, and ethnic groups. Low-power TV stations will be affordable; a no-frills version may cost less than $120 000 — about 5 percent of the cost of a conventional station. With their limited range, low-power TV stations can be designed so as not to interfere with conventional stations.

articleTitle: Communications: The quandary of office automation: Systems designers are heatedly debating the most efficient communication hardware for the electronic office of the future
abstract: Although the building blocks for the “electronic office of the future” — the work stations, processors, and software — can now be delivered, systems integrators have long debated the most efficient communications hardware for linking them together. Should it be a local area network, which transmits baseband or broadband signals through high-speed coaxial cables — but still has one foot in the laboratory? Or should it be the slower PABX, or private automatic branch exchange: a computer-controlled switch that uses that old reliable, the telephone system, to route voice or data signals in analog or digital form?

articleTitle: Computers: The gread weather network: Weather forecasting can be improved through better models and speedier reporting
abstract: Meteorologists in the Boston office of the U.S. Weather Service were tracking a storm in the Atlantic, centered about 300 miles east of Norfolk, Va. Satellite images and computer-based forecasts from the National Meteorological Center in Washington, D, C., indicated the storm would move northeast in the ocean and pass well east of Boston. With this information, the Boston forecasters issued a local prediction of 2 to 4 inches of snow for the next day, Sunday, December 6, 1981.

articleTitle: Communications: AT&T plans ahead: The telecommunications giant will enter the commercial marketplace, drawing on its traditional technical strengths
abstract: After being in unchallenged control of 80 percent of all local telephone service in the United States for decades, the American Telephone & Telegraph Co. is preparing to lay aside that dominant role and enter such formerly forbidden marketing waters as data processing, computer communications, and telephone and computer-terminal equipment. All are areas from which it once was barred by Federal regulations. The radical shift, which will put the company in competition with International Business Machines Corp., Xerox Corp., Digital Equipment Corp., and other formidable rivals is based on the agreement last January between AT&T and the U.S. Department of Justice.

articleTitle: New product applications: Logic analyzer displays data in three colors, offers up to 104 channels of data acquisition
abstract: The CAS 9120 series of color logic analyzers - like the entire CAS9100 family - is a modular digital analysis system that houses both data-acqulsttlon and patterngenerationcardmodules in the same mainframe.

articleTitle: New product applications: Array processor performs 5 million floating-point operations per second, has 200-ns operation time
abstract: The MSP-3000 floating-point array processor Is compatible with Digital Equipment Corp. minicomputers. It uses the DEC 32-bit floating-point format for data input, output, and processing. Constructed on six circuit boards and designed around an integral minicomputer and a 64-kilobyte to 2-megabyte dual-ported memory, it can. compute a complex multiplication in 16 microseconds or a 1024-point fast-Fourier transform (FFT) in 7.0 ms. Basic operation time is 200 ns.

articleTitle: New product applications: EJAO-size drafting plotter permits programmed selection of up to eight pens, operates at speeds to 60 cmls
abstract: The HP 7585A is a E/AO-size drafting plotter with microprocessor control, 4-g acceleration, and speeds up to 60 cm/s. It can generate drawings in any size from 203 by 267 mm to 927 by 1189 mm.

articleTitle: New product applications: Slngl-hlp mieroprocessor compriese 16-bit CPU clock generator, two DMA channels, and programmable inienupt controller
abstract: The 80186 chip contains a single 16-bit CPU and all functions commonly found in a single-board CPU subsystem.

articleTitle: Careers: We look at ourselves: The manufacturing engineer: The best ones are good planners and organizers, with a knack for interfacing with multidisciplined individuals
abstract: Manufacturing engineers come in as many different packages as the products they produce. They can be young men and women working as supervisors and troubleshooters at manufacturing stations. They can be older people in management, overseeing such operations as scheduling manufacturing, holding down costs, and requisitioning tools and labor. They may work for a company that produces large, sophisticated, multimillion-dollar electronic systems. Or they may be involved in the production of simple discrete components, electronic modules, or solid-state chips. But one thing they all have in common is that they are primarily concerned with the fabrication, testing, and assembly of a system or product that has already been designed. Only rarely are they involved in the initial design concept. They also share the following characteristics: • They interface with an unusually large number of multidisciplined people in and out of their own company. • They manage and motivate people and at the same time should have a knack for recognizing good suggestions about improving products, systems, or production operations. • They are good planners and organizers.

articleTitle: Today's air force: The chips are flying
abstract: Since World War I, when aircraft first flew in combat, military leaders have realized that air superiority can spell the difference between victory and defeat on the ground or at sea. Advancing troop columns can be cut down by strafing aircraft, command posts and other targets can be bombed, and in World War II the most heavily armored battleships were sunk by air attack. The balance between British Harriers and Argentine Skyhawks was crucial to the recent Falklands conflict: had the Argentines possessed longer-range aircraft, armed with more modern weapons like the Exocet, or had the British possessed long-range surveillance planes and supersonic interceptors, the pattern of losses might have been far different.

articleTitle: Entertainment/control technology: The wonderful world of Epcot: Walt Disney Productions unveils a futuristic amusement park that may be even more intriguing to engineers than to the public at large
abstract: Forget Carl Sagan. He just explains the universe. Jacob Bronowski merely told us about the ascent of man. But the late Walt Disney, the greatest science popularizer of them all, thought big. Thanks to his vision, Walt Disney Productions will introduce the public this fall to the world of tomorrow — and not just in books, but in his inimitable style of animation and recreation.

articleTitle: II. Design: High technology, low cost
abstract: A roomful of engineers watch the flight of a rocket on a small video screen. They control it with the help of a supercomputer. The year is 1969. The experience was to cost the United States $300 million. The goal was to put a man on the moon-money was no object.

articleTitle: New product applications: Controller supports up to eight array processors, each transferring at the maximum 3-megabyte-per-second rate
abstract: The DPS-2400 controller increases the capabilities of array processors. It interfaces with a PDP or VAX computer and functions as the central node of a computational and data-flow subsystem that integrates array processors, mass memory, and peripheral storage devices. Its control, memory, and data-transfer resources keep multiple attached processors operating at full capacity.

articleTitle: Management: Six steps to becoming a successful entrepreneur: Starting one's own business requires both capital and a `feeling' knowing how others did it may help
abstract: Since the 1947 invention of the transistor at Bell Laboratories and the subsequent formation of the Shockley Transistor Co. by one of the inventors, William Shockley, engineers with ideas for new products, new markets, or new methods of management have left secure positions to start their own companies. Engineers exploiting breakthroughs in semiconductor manufacturing, computers, computer peripherals, lasers, and other electronic fields have ended up as presidents of their own multimillion-dollar corporations.

articleTitle: War 4: Major power strategies: The U.S. debates disarmament strategies, and NATO's readiness, while the USSR promises no first use: The superpowers: Nuclear at issue
abstract: The ongoing debate in the past year over the military strategy of the United States and its allies has spilled out of the military journals and onto the front pages of newspapers. The key questions of nuclear policy that have been argued for years in the classified conferences of specialists are the subject of mass demonstrations in Europe, Japan, and North America. What has brought the once-arcane discussion of nuclear planning to the attention of much of the world's population is the adoption by the current U.S. Administration of a new military strategy that calls for a vast arms buildup.
